messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Keoni sat in the clinic waiting room with his hands pressed flat on his thighs, trying not to look at the door every time it opened. At sixty-three, he had spent most of his adult life moving through crowded community meetings, standing at podiums, talking face-to-face with neighbors about zoning laws and school funding. Now the simplest interaction—someone raising their voice to make a point, even calmly—sent a wash of heat up his neck and made his chest tighten as if he were about to be struck. He had no idea how to explain that to the therapist.

The accident happened three years ago, on a Tuesday evening in late spring. Keoni had been driving home from a neighborhood coalition meeting, tired but satisfied. At a four-way intersection, a truck ran the red light and T-boned his sedan. The impact spun the car into a utility pole. What Keoni remembered with excruciating clarity was the sound—metal tearing, glass exploding—and then the face of the other driver, a man in a deputy sheriff's uniform, who got out of the truck and started shouting. The man was furious, yelling that Keoni had come out of nowhere, that it was his fault. In that moment, Keoni could not speak. He could not move. His left arm was broken, his ribs cracked, and he was bleeding internally, but what stayed with him was the rage in the other man's voice and the insignia on his collar. Other parts of the crash were simply gone. He could not remember the seconds before impact no matter how hard he tried. He knew he had seen the truck coming, but the memory would not come. When he tried to tell his sister about it later, the words would not form. He knew what had happened, but his mouth would not cooperate; he could only gesture and shake his head.

In the weeks that followed, Keoni told himself the accident was his fault. If he had looked left one more time, if he had slowed down, if he had not been so tired, the truck would have missed him. That thought looped daily, even though the police report placed blame on the other driver. He began to notice that his body did not believe he was safe. At home, alone in his small apartment (his divorce had been final for a decade), he would hear a car horn outside and find himself on the floor, heart hammering, before he knew what he was doing. He had come to believe that his own body was his enemy, that it kept reacting as if the crash were still happening, that it would betray him at any moment. And underneath that was a deadness he could not shake. He felt hollow, numb, as if something vital inside him had been scooped out.

The triggers narrowed his world. At community meetings, which used to be his lifeblood, someone would express frustration about a pothole or a broken streetlight, and Keoni would see the deputy's face again, hear that tone, and his mind would blank. He stopped attending. He dodged phone calls from colleagues. He took different routes to the grocery store to avoid passing the sheriff's substation. The sight of a uniform—any uniform, even a security guard at the mall—made his stomach drop. His work as a community organizer had always depended on his presence, his voice, his willingness to sit with anger and turn it into action. Now anger itself, even when it was calm and directed elsewhere, felt like a threat. His absence became noticeable. A coalition he had helped build for fifteen years lost momentum without him. His colleagues assumed he was sick or burned out. He could not correct them because he could not find the words.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a single moment. A young mother he had mentored for years called him, asking for help with a school board issue. She said she needed him, and he heard the frustration in her voice—not angry, just urgent—and he hung up. Then he sat in his kitchen and wept. The next morning he called his primary care doctor and asked for a referral. He did not know if talking would make the memories clearer or fill in the blanks he had learned to live around. He did not know if he could describe the accident at all. But he knew he could not keep watching his life shrink into the space between his couch and his front door. What he hoped most was to feel something again, even if it hurt. What he feared most was that the numbness was all that was left.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts: The vignette does not describe unwanted thoughts about the trauma as a trigger; it describes flashbacks and memories upon specific triggers but not intrusive thoughts independently.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.
